title: Meta’s MTIA Custom AI Silicon at Hot Chips 2026
gist: Meta laid out its four-generation MTIA roadmap (300/400/450/500), explaining that MTIA 300 was purpose-built to beat GPUs on Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM) training TCO with a 1.8x forward/backward speedup, while MTIA 400 pivots to broad GenAI inference with MXFP4 support, chiplet-based scaling to a 72-ASIC domain, and massive generational jumps versus MTIA 200 (15x FP16 compute, 46x DRAM bandwidth, 5x SRAM bandwidth) — with AI accelerators explicitly noted as now the largest track at Hot Chips, having overtaken CPUs.

themes.theme: AI accelerators overtaking CPUs as the industry's center of gravity

insights.claim: AI accelerators have become the largest technical track at Hot Chips 2026, overtaking CPUs, reflecting how much engineering investment the industry has poured into AI-specific silicon.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A structural shift in conference/industry attention from general-purpose CPUs to domain-specific AI accelerators signals where R&D capital and talent are concentrating industry-wide — a leading indicator that custom AI silicon investment (not just GPU purchases) will keep growing across all major tech companies.
insights.quote: Once a part of the GPU track, AI accelerators have become the largest track at the show – overtaking CPUs – underscoring just how much in the way of engineering resources have been invested into the chips.
insights.locator: Kicking off the afternoon presentation blocks

insights.claim: Meta's custom silicon strategy is explicitly framed as getting away from buying commodity hardware from major vendors (i.e., Nvidia) and avoiding the margins that entails, driven by expected massive internal demand for AI inference capacity.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Direct confirmation that Meta's custom silicon program is a deliberate margin-capture strategy against Nvidia's GPU pricing, reinforcing the broader thesis that hyperscaler custom-ASIC programs are a structural long-term headwind to Nvidia's addressable market share of AI inference workloads specifically.
insights.quote: the emphasis is on producing in-house silicon that is better aligned to the workloads they are expecting, and getting away from buying commodity hardware from the major vendors and paying the margins that entails.
insights.locator: First up on the AI track is meta

themes.theme: MTIA 300: beating GPUs on DLRM training economics

insights.claim: Meta developed MTIA specifically because GPUs are not ideal for Deep Learning Recommendation Model (DLRM) training — DLRM's extreme memory-boundedness creates GPU utilization bottlenecks, compounded by the total cost of ownership of operating fleets of GPUs for this workload.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, well-defined workload (recommendation model training) where GPUs are structurally mismatched, explaining why Meta — despite also being one of the largest Nvidia GPU buyers — still invests heavily in a separate custom chip specifically for this use case rather than just buying more GPUs.
insights.quote: GPUs are not ideal for DLRM training, in Meta's eyes. Memory and FLOPS utilization challenges present bottlenecks to training. Not to mention the TCO of operating all of those GPUs.

insights.claim: MTIA 300 (72 processing elements, 16 messaging elements, 216GB HBM3e, 3nm compute die / 5nm I/O die) achieved parity with GPUs at competitive TCO and delivered over a 1.8x speedup in both forward and backward propagation versus GPUs on Meta's recommendation workloads.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete >1.8x performance advantage plus TCO parity is a measurable proof point that Meta's custom silicon bet paid off on its first purpose-built training chip, validating the broader industry thesis that workload-specific ASICs can beat general-purpose GPUs on both cost and speed for well-defined workloads.
insights.quote: The high memory and cache bandwidth of the chip, along with purpose-built units, helped them net an over 1.8x speedup in both forward and backwards propagating models.

themes.theme: MTIA 400: pivot to broad GenAI inference

insights.claim: MTIA 400 marks a strategic pivot back to being an inference chip (after MTIA 300 focused on DLRM training), but this time designed for a much broader class of inference beyond just recommendations, driven by GenAI's need for immense compute throughput, efficient multi-accelerator scaling, and ever-growing memory capacity requirements.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Shows Meta's custom silicon roadmap evolving in lockstep with its own product mix shift from recommendation-heavy workloads toward GenAI — an internal signal of how much of Meta's compute budget is now GenAI-driven versus classic recommendation-system inference.
insights.quote: the company has applied those learnings to the MTIA 400, which goes back to being an inference chip... not just for recommendations, but is designed to handle a broader case of inference.

insights.claim: MTIA 400 adds hardware MXFP4 support (a microscaling FP4 format with shared exponent for higher effective precision) plus new MX8/MX8S 16x16 FP8 block formats for training, directly boosting achievable FLOPS.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: MXFP4/microscaling adoption puts Meta's silicon roadmap in line with the same low-precision compute trend driving Nvidia Blackwell/Rubin, Google TPU 8t, and OpenAI Jalapeno — confirming FP4-class microscaling formats are becoming the default currency of AI accelerator throughput industry-wide.
insights.quote: Hardware MXFP4 support is also a big boon in helping Meta push a larger number of FLOPS.

insights.claim: MTIA 400 moves to a more disaggregated chiplet design with distinct compute, SoC, and I/O chiplet types (2 compute chiplets, HBM stacks alongside, an SoC chiplet at top for PCIe Gen6 host connection, and two networking chiplets at the bottom), and introduces two new types of embedding caches for DLRM.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Increased chiplet disaggregation (mirroring the industry-wide move toward multi-die packages) suggests rising reliance on advanced packaging (CoWoS-class technology) for Meta's silicon supply chain, relevant to demand modeling for TSMC advanced packaging capacity.
insights.quote: They are not just using chiplets here, but now an even larger number of chiplet types, with compute, SoC, and I/O chipets.

insights.claim: MTIA 400 introduces a Host Embedding Cache (HEC) specifically to manage the extremely large size of Meta's recommendation embedding tables by keeping the 'hot' portions close to the accelerators, backed by 8 stacks of HBM3e delivering 9.4TB/second of memory bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A dedicated embedding-cache hierarchy is a Meta-specific architectural response to its uniquely large-scale recommendation system embedding tables — a design choice unlikely to be replicated by non-recommendation-heavy AI companies, underscoring how workload-specific Meta's silicon really is versus general-purpose GPU alternatives.
insights.quote: This also covers the host embedding cache (HEC), which helps Meta manage the extremely large size of their embedding tables by keeping the hot portions close to the accelerators.

insights.claim: MTIA 400's scale-up fabric uses Ethernet-based networking offering 1.2TB/second of bandwidth and scales to 72 ASICs in a single scale-up domain (4 accelerators per tray), with scale-out networking handled through a PCIe switch, emphasizing elimination of unnecessary data movement via AllReduce/AllToAll support.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Meta's choice of Ethernet-based scale-up (rather than a proprietary interconnect like NVLink) echoes Microsoft Maia's all-Ethernet approach — a recurring cross-vendor pattern suggesting hyperscalers are converging on Ethernet as the preferred scale-up fabric for custom silicon to avoid dependency on Nvidia's proprietary NVLink IP.
insights.quote: The Ethernet-based scale-up fabric of the chip offers 1.2TB/second of bandwidth, while scale-out networking takes place through the PCIe switch.

insights.claim: Versus its predecessor MTIA 200, the MTIA 400 delivers over 15x the FP16 compute, a 46x increase in DRAM bandwidth, and 5x the SRAM bandwidth, with a single accelerator offering 12 PFLOPS of FP4 performance.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: A 46x DRAM bandwidth jump in one generation is an extraordinary leap (far beyond typical Moore's-law-paced gains), signaling how aggressively Meta is re-architecting its silicon roadmap specifically to meet GenAI-driven memory demands rather than incremental scaling.
insights.quote: this is over 15x the FP16 compute and a whopping 46x increase in DRAM bandwidth. Not to mention 5x as much SRAM bandwidth.

insights.claim: Each processing element (PE) in MTIA 400 contains two RISC-V-based CPU-P cores (with both scalar and vector units) for general-purpose vector operations, and a dedicated special function unit (SFU) handles non-GEMM workloads including a gather operation that can pull 64 elements in a single cycle.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Meta's use of RISC-V cores embedded throughout the chip (both in PEs and messaging elements) signals RISC-V is becoming the default 'glue' ISA of choice for custom AI silicon control logic, relevant to RISC-V ecosystem investment theses versus Arm licensing.
insights.quote: These CPU-P cores are RISC-V based, and contain both a scalar and vector cores, for general purpose vector operations.

insights.claim: Meta's roadmap already has MTIA 450 in development to enhance GenAI inference performance further, while MTIA 500 will focus on scaling beyond the current 72-ASIC single scale-up domain, matching the broader industry push toward ever-larger scale-up domains.
insights.speaker: Ryan Smith
insights.so_what: Confirms Meta is committing to a multi-year, multi-generation custom silicon roadmap (not a one-off experiment), and that domain-size scaling beyond 72 ASICs is an explicit near-term target — a leading indicator of Meta's future networking/interconnect capital investment needs.
insights.quote: The 450 offers enhanced GenAI inference performance, while the 500 will focus even more on scaling, matching the broader industry push towards larger scale-up domains going beyond just 72 ASICs in a single domain.
